content:
A New Mexico state judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion to the state — one of the largest financial penalties ever imposed on a company in American legal history. District Court Judge Francis Mathew issued the order on Wednesday, October 21, after a jury found that the company systematically misled consumers about the privacy of their data.

The case traces back to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The company, then known as Facebook, disclosed in 2018 that the personal information of as many as 87 million Facebook users had been improperly harvested by the British political consulting firm — which worked on Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign — through a third-party app, and used to build profiles of American voters.

New Mexico’s attorney general sued in 2021, accusing Meta of lying to Facebook users in the state about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation, and other internal policies. The state alleged that Meta knew third parties had broad access to users’ personal data and tolerated hate speech and other harmful content when it benefited the company’s bottom line.

The numbers behind the ruling

In September, a jury found Meta liable for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act. State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 per violation — Judge Mathew calculated that more than $219 billion was warranted, but reduced the figure to $25 billion. State lawyers had sought between $35 billion and $40 billion.

“Facebook’s wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Mathew wrote in his 20-page order. He described what he called a “coherent strategy designed to mislead the public” and “systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model.”

“Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception,” the judge wrote.

Both sides speak

Attorney General Raúl Torrez said technology companies should treat the verdict as a warning. “For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Torrez said in a statement. “This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal. It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences.” Under New Mexico law, fines for violations of consumer protection laws fund state education.

Meta says it will appeal. Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement: “This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico. At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”

Why this matters here: millions of Webb County residents use Facebook and Instagram every day — including to read this site. A jury found the company’s claims about user privacy were not honest. The appeal will decide whether the $25 billion stands, but the finding itself is on the record.

title: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion to New Mexico After Jury Finds Company Misled Users on Privacy
